title: 19yo F Diabetic Ketoacidosis
background: First year university student. Four weeks of thirst, frequent urination and 6 kg weight loss that she attributed to exam stress. Two days of vomiting and diffuse abdominal pain, and today she became too drowsy to attend class. No known diabetes and no family history. No alcohol. Last menstrual period 3 weeks ago. Her roommate says she has been breathing strangely since this morning.

exam.finding: Thin, drowsy but rousable, deep sighing Kussmaul respirations, fruity acetone odour on the breath
Dry cracked lips, tacky mucous membranes, sunken eyes, no oral thrush, no neck stiffness
Sinus tachycardia, low volume pulse, capillary refill 3 seconds, JVP not visible, no murmur
Clear breath sounds bilaterally, deep and rapid regular respirations, no crackles or wheeze
Diffuse tenderness without rebound or guarding, no localisation to McBurney's point, sluggish bowel sounds, no organomegaly
Reduced turgor with skin tenting over the sternum, cool dry peripheries, no rash or infected wound, no injection sites
GCS 14 (E3V5M6), slow to answer but orientated, no focal deficit, pupils 3 mm equal and reactive, no papilloedema

investigations.name: Venous blood gas
investigations.report: Severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis with maximal respiratory compensation. This meets severe DKA criteria.

investigations.name: Beta-hydroxybutyrate
investigations.report: Marked ketonaemia. Use this rather than urine ketones to track clearance.

investigations.name: Potassium
investigations.report: Measured potassium is high but total body potassium is severely depleted. It will fall sharply once insulin starts.

investigations.name: Sodium
investigations.report: Pseudohyponatraemia from hyperglycaemia. Corrected sodium is approximately 135 mmol/L.

investigations.name: Creatinine
investigations.report: Pre-renal acute kidney injury from volume depletion. Anion gap 30 mmol/L.

investigations.name: 12-Lead ECG
investigations.report: Sinus tachycardia at 122/min. Tall peaked T waves in V2 to V4 consistent with hyperkalaemia. Normal QRS duration. No ischaemic changes.

investigations.name: Urinalysis
investigations.value: Ketones 4+, glucose 4+, nitrite negative, leucocyte esterase negative
investigations.report: Ketonuria and glycosuria. No evidence of urinary tract infection as a precipitant.

investigations.name: White cell count
investigations.report: Leucocytosis is common in DKA itself. Only pursue infection if there is fever, a source, or a left shift with bands.

investigations.name: HbA1c
investigations.report: Confirms months of untreated hyperglycaemia, consistent with new onset type 1 diabetes.

data.label: IV access, point of care glucose, ketones and venous gas with potassium
Fluid resuscitation first, before any insulin

doseMap.Normal saline bolus: 15-20 mL/kg (about 1000 mL) over the first hour, then 250-500 mL/h guided by perfusion

data.label: Perfusion improves
data.narrative: After the first litre she is more alert and her peripheries warm up. Glucose has already fallen to 448 mg/dL from dilution and renal clearance alone.

data.label: Sit down and tell her she has newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, and call her parents with her permission (Empathy)
data.narrative: You explain the diagnosis in plain language before the insulin drip starts, and ask what she wants her parents told. She cries, then asks good questions about whether she can still go back to class. Nurse Ann arranges the diabetes nurse educator for the morning. Dr. Bob mutters that the ward can do that later.

data.label: Check potassium before starting insulin and replace as needed

doseMap.Potassium chloride in maintenance fluid: If K 3.3-5.3 mmol/L add 20-30 mmol/L to the fluid. If K below 3.3 mmol/L hold insulin and replace first. If above 5.3 mmol/L give no potassium and recheck in 2 hours

data.label: Fixed rate insulin infusion, no bolus

doseMap.Regular insulin IV infusion: 0.1 units/kg/h continuous (about 5 units/h). A bolus adds no benefit and increases the risk of hypokalaemia and cerebral oedema

data.label: Hourly monitoring and add dextrose when glucose falls below 250 mg/dL

doseMap.5% or 10% dextrose co-infusion: Start when glucose is below 250 mg/dL, keep the insulin running to clear ketones. Aim for a fall in glucose of 50-75 mg/dL per hour

data.label: Acidosis clearing
data.narrative: At six hours pH is 7.28, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 1.9 mmol/L and potassium 3.9 mmol/L on replacement. Kussmaul breathing has stopped. You did not give bicarbonate, which is correct at this pH.

data.label: Transition to subcutaneous insulin only after resolution criteria are met
actions: Overlap 1-2 hours before stopping the infusion

doseMap.Long acting subcutaneous insulin: Give 1-2 hours before stopping the drip. Resolution means anion gap under 12, bicarbonate at least 15 and beta-hydroxybutyrate under 0.6 with the patient eating

data.label: Disposition
data.narrative: She is admitted to the medical ward on a basal bolus regimen. The diabetes educator starts carbohydrate counting and injection technique before discharge. No cerebral oedema, no hypokalaemic arrhythmia.
